title: Generalized Eigenspaces
---

The shear $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{psmallmatrix}$ has too few eigenvectors to be diagonalizable. To decompose such operators we enlarge the eigenspaces, admitting vectors that are not eigenvectors but are killed by some power of $\varphi - \lambda$. It is simplest to start with the eigenvalue $0$, where the relevant operator is $\varphi$ itself.

## <span class="num">7.6.1</span> Generalized Kernels

:::definition{7.6.1} Generalized kernel
The ***generalized kernel*** of $\varphi \in \End(V)$ is $$\gker(\varphi) = \{v \in V : \varphi^m(v) = 0 \text{ for some } m \geq 1\}.$$ These are all the vectors that are eventually sent to $0$ by repeatedly applying $\varphi$.
:::

:::note
The notation $\gker(\varphi)$ is Auroux’s; it is not standard.
:::

The difference between the kernel and the generalized kernel can be summed up as follows: a vector is in the kernel if one application of $\varphi$ sends it to $0$, and in the generalized kernel if some number of applications does. If $\varphi^m(v) = 0$, then also $\varphi^{m+1}(v) = 0$, so the kernels of the powers of $\varphi$ form an increasing chain $$\{0\} = \ker(\varphi^0) \subseteq \ker(\varphi) \subseteq \ker(\varphi^2) \subseteq \ker(\varphi^3) \subseteq \cdots,$$ and $\gker(\varphi)$ is their union. The union of an increasing chain of subspaces is a subspace, so $\gker(\varphi)$ is a subspace of $V$.

:::proposition{7.6.2} Stabilization of kernels
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. If $\ker(\varphi^m) = \ker(\varphi^{m+1})$ for some $m \geq 0$, then $\ker(\varphi^{m+j}) = \ker(\varphi^m)$ for all $j \geq 0$, and $\gker(\varphi) = \ker(\varphi^m)$.
2. If $V$ is finite-dimensional with $\dim V = n$, then $\ker(\varphi^n) = \ker(\varphi^{n+1})$, and hence $\gker(\varphi) = \ker(\varphi^n)$.
:::

:::proof
(a) We show $\ker(\varphi^{m+2}) = \ker(\varphi^{m+1})$; repeating the argument gives the rest. The inclusion $\supseteq$ always holds. If $\varphi^{m+2}(v) = 0$, then $\varphi^{m+1}(\varphi(v)) = 0$, so $\varphi(v) \in \ker(\varphi^{m+1}) = \ker(\varphi^m)$. Hence $\varphi^{m+1}(v) = \varphi^m(\varphi(v)) = 0$. So the chain is constant from $\ker(\varphi^m)$ on, and its union is $\ker(\varphi^m)$.

(b) Let $d_j = \dim \ker(\varphi^j)$. If $\ker(\varphi^j) = \ker(\varphi^{j+1})$ for some $j < n$, then (a) gives $\ker(\varphi^n) = \ker(\varphi^{n+1})$. Otherwise each inclusion $\ker(\varphi^j) \subsetneq \ker(\varphi^{j+1})$ for $j < n$ is strict, so $0 = d_0 < d_1 < \cdots < d_n$, whence $d_n \geq n$ and $\ker(\varphi^n) = V$; then also $\ker(\varphi^{n+1}) = V$.
:::

:::example{7.6.3}
Let $\varphi : k^2 \to k^2$ be given by $e_1 \mapsto 0$, $e_2 \mapsto e_1$, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $\ker(\varphi) = k \cdot e_1$, but $\ker(\varphi^2) = \gker(\varphi) = k^2$. Note also that $\Img(\varphi) = k \cdot e_1 = \ker(\varphi)$, so $V \neq \ker(\varphi) \oplus \Img(\varphi)$ here.
:::

:::definition{7.6.4} Nilpotent operator
An operator $\varphi \in \End(V)$ is ***nilpotent*** if $\varphi^m = 0$ for some positive integer $m$. Then $\gker(\varphi) = V$. When $V$ is finite-dimensional the converse holds, because $\gker(\varphi) = \ker(\varphi^{\dim V})$ by Proposition [7.6.2](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-2)(b). If $V \neq \{0\}$, the smallest such $m$ is called the ***index of nilpotency*** of $\varphi$.
:::

As the example shows, in general $V \neq \ker(\varphi) \oplus \Img(\varphi)$. Replacing $\varphi$ by a high enough power repairs this:

:::lemma{7.6.5} Kernel–image decomposition for a power
Let $V$ be finite-dimensional, $\varphi \in \End(V)$, and let $m \geq 0$ satisfy $\ker(\varphi^m) = \ker(\varphi^{m+1})$ (for example $m = \dim V$). Then $$V = \ker(\varphi^m) \oplus \Img(\varphi^m),$$ both summands are $\varphi$-invariant, and $\varphi$ restricts to an isomorphism of $\Img(\varphi^m)$ onto itself. In particular, $V = \gker(\varphi) \oplus \Img(\varphi^{\dim V})$.
:::

:::proof
Both summands are $\varphi$-invariant by Proposition [7.3.3](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#proposition-7-3-3).

**Intersection is trivial:** Suppose $v \in \ker(\varphi^m) \cap \Img(\varphi^m)$. Write $v = \varphi^m(u)$ for some $u \in V$. Then $\varphi^{2m}(u) = \varphi^m(v) = 0$, so $u \in \ker(\varphi^{2m}) = \ker(\varphi^m)$ by Proposition [7.6.2](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-2)(a). Thus $v = \varphi^m(u) = 0$.

**Sum is all of $V$:** By Rank–Nullity applied to $\varphi^m$, $\dim V = \dim \ker(\varphi^m) + \dim \Img(\varphi^m)$. Since the intersection is trivial, the sum $\ker(\varphi^m) + \Img(\varphi^m)$ is direct and has dimension $\dim V$. Hence it equals $V$.

**Restriction to the image:** The kernel of $\varphi|_{\Img(\varphi^m)}$ is $\ker(\varphi) \cap \Img(\varphi^m) \subseteq \ker(\varphi^m) \cap \Img(\varphi^m) = \{0\}$ (here $\ker(\varphi) \subseteq \ker(\varphi^{m+1}) = \ker(\varphi^m)$). An injective operator on a finite-dimensional space is an isomorphism (Corollary [6.1.16](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#corollary-6-1-16)).

The last sentence follows from Proposition [7.6.2](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-2)(b).
:::

:::note
This decomposition is the key structural result for understanding non-diagonalizable operators. The generalized kernel $\gker(\varphi)$ captures the “nilpotent part” of $\varphi$: the restriction of $\varphi$ to it is nilpotent. On the complementary invariant subspace $\Img(\varphi^m)$, the restriction of $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
:::

## <span class="num">7.6.2</span> Generalized Eigenspaces

Now we apply the same idea to $\varphi - \lambda$ for an arbitrary scalar $\lambda$. From now on in this section, $V$ is finite-dimensional with $\dim V = n$.

:::definition{7.6.6} Generalized eigenspace
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ and $\lambda \in k$. Set $$V_\lambda = \gker(\varphi - \lambda) = \{v \in V : (\varphi - \lambda)^m(v) = 0 \text{ for some } m \geq 1\} = \ker(\varphi - \lambda)^n,$$ the last equality by Proposition [7.6.2](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-2)(b). A nonzero vector of $V_\lambda$ is a ***generalized eigenvector*** of $\varphi$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. When $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\varphi$, $V_\lambda$ is called the ***generalized eigenspace*** of $\varphi$ for $\lambda$.
:::

:::note
Every eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$ is a generalized eigenvector, since $E(\lambda, \varphi) = \ker(\varphi - \lambda) \subseteq V_\lambda$; but $V_\lambda$ may be strictly larger. Its elements are the vectors that are “eventually killed” by $\varphi - \lambda$.
:::

:::example{7.6.7} Generalized eigenspace of the shear
Recall the shear $\varphi : \RR^2 \to \RR^2$ with matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The only eigenvalue is $\lambda = 1$, and the eigenspace is $E(1, \varphi) = \ker(A - I) = \ker\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \operatorname{Span}\{e_1\}$, which is one-dimensional.

However, $(A - I)^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = 0$.

So the generalized eigenspace is $V_1 = \ker(A - I)^2 = \RR^2$. The vector $e_2$ is a generalized eigenvector that is not an eigenvector: $(A - I)e_2 = e_1 \neq 0$, but $(A - I)^2 e_2 = 0$.
:::

:::proposition{7.6.8} Basic properties of generalized eigenspaces
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ and $\lambda, \mu \in k$. Then:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $E(\lambda, \varphi) \subseteq V_\lambda$, and $V_\lambda \neq \{0\}$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $\varphi$.
2. $V_\lambda$ is $\varphi$-invariant.
3. The restriction of $\varphi - \lambda$ to $V_\lambda$ is nilpotent.
4. If $\mu \neq \lambda$, the restriction of $\varphi - \mu$ to $V_\lambda$ is invertible. Consequently $V_\lambda \cap V_\mu = \{0\}$, and if $V_\lambda \neq \{0\}$, the only eigenvalue of $\varphi|_{V_\lambda}$ is $\lambda$.
:::

:::proof
(a) The inclusion is clear. If $v \in V_\lambda$ is nonzero, let $r \geq 0$ be the largest integer with $w = (\varphi - \lambda)^r(v) \neq 0$; then $(\varphi - \lambda)(w) = 0$, so $w$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Conversely, an eigenvector lies in $E(\lambda, \varphi) \subseteq V_\lambda$.

(b) $V_\lambda = \ker\bigl((\varphi - \lambda)^n\bigr)$ and $(\varphi - \lambda)^n$ is a polynomial in $\varphi$, so this is Proposition [7.3.3](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#proposition-7-3-3).

(c) By definition $(\varphi - \lambda)^n$ is zero on $V_\lambda$, and $V_\lambda$ is invariant under $\varphi - \lambda$ by (b).

(d) Let $v \in V_\lambda$ with $(\varphi - \mu)(v) = 0$. Then $(\varphi - \lambda)(v) = (\mu - \lambda)v$, so $0 = (\varphi - \lambda)^n(v) = (\mu - \lambda)^n v$. As $\mu - \lambda \neq 0$, we get $v = 0$. Thus $\varphi - \mu$ is injective on the invariant finite-dimensional subspace $V_\lambda$, hence invertible there (Corollary [6.1.16](/notes/math-55a/6-1-kernel-and-image#corollary-6-1-16)). Then $(\varphi - \mu)^n$ is injective on $V_\lambda$ too; since it kills $V_\mu$, we get $V_\lambda \cap V_\mu = \{0\}$. Finally, an eigenvalue $\mu$ of $\varphi|_{V_\lambda}$ is a scalar for which $\varphi - \mu$ is not injective on $V_\lambda$, so $\mu = \lambda$.
:::

:::proposition{7.6.9} Invariant splitting
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ and $\lambda \in k$, and put $W_\lambda = \Img(\varphi - \lambda)^n$. Then $$V = V_\lambda \oplus W_\lambda,$$ both summands are $\varphi$-invariant, and $\varphi - \lambda$ restricts to an isomorphism of $W_\lambda$ onto itself. In particular, $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $\varphi|_{W_\lambda}$.
:::

:::proof
Apply Lemma [7.6.5](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#lemma-7-6-5) to the operator $\varphi - \lambda$ with $m = n$. This gives $V = \ker(\varphi - \lambda)^n \oplus \Img(\varphi - \lambda)^n = V_\lambda \oplus W_\lambda$ and the statement about $\varphi - \lambda$ on $W_\lambda$. Both summands are kernels or images of a polynomial in $\varphi$, so they are $\varphi$-invariant (Proposition [7.3.3](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#proposition-7-3-3)).
:::

:::proposition{7.6.10} Independence of generalized eigenspaces
Let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_\ell \in k$ be distinct. If $v_1 + \cdots + v_\ell = 0$ with $v_i \in V_{\lambda_i}$, then $v_i = 0$ for all $i$. That is, the sum $V_{\lambda_1} + \cdots + V_{\lambda_\ell}$ is direct.
:::

:::proof
We show $v_1 = 0$; the same argument applies to every $v_i$. Suppose $v_1 \neq 0$, and let $r \geq 0$ be the largest integer with $w = (\varphi - \lambda_1)^r(v_1) \neq 0$. Then $(\varphi - \lambda_1)(w) = 0$, i.e., $\varphi(w) = \lambda_1 w$. Consider the operator $$T = (\varphi - \lambda_2)^n \circ \cdots \circ (\varphi - \lambda_\ell)^n \circ (\varphi - \lambda_1)^r.$$ Its factors commute (Proposition [7.2.2](/notes/math-55a/7-2-polynomials-in-an-operator#proposition-7-2-2)). For $j \geq 2$, $T(v_j) = 0$, because we may apply $(\varphi - \lambda_j)^n$ first and $(\varphi - \lambda_j)^n(v_j) = 0$. On the other hand, $(\varphi - \lambda_j)(w) = (\lambda_1 - \lambda_j)w$, so $$T(v_1) = (\varphi - \lambda_2)^n \circ \cdots \circ (\varphi - \lambda_\ell)^n (w) = \prod_{j=2}^{\ell} (\lambda_1 - \lambda_j)^n \, w \neq 0.$$ Applying $T$ to $v_1 + \cdots + v_\ell = 0$ gives $T(v_1) = 0$, a contradiction. Hence $v_1 = 0$.
:::

## <span class="num">7.6.3</span> The Generalized Eigenspace Decomposition

The following theorem is the main structural result for operators on finite-dimensional vector spaces over algebraically closed fields. Its proof is an induction on the dimension built on the invariant splitting, and it does not use the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem.

:::theorem{7.6.11} Generalized eigenspace decomposition
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field $k$, and let $\varphi \in \End(V)$. Let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_\ell$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $\varphi$. Then $$V = V_{\lambda_1} \oplus V_{\lambda_2} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{\lambda_\ell}.$$ In particular, $\sum_{i=1}^\ell \dim V_{\lambda_i} = \dim V$.
:::

:::proof
By Proposition [7.6.10](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-10), the sum of the $V_{\lambda_i}$ is direct, so it remains to show that they span $V$. We use induction on $\dim V$. If $V = \{0\}$, there is nothing to prove.

Let $\dim V = n \geq 1$ and assume the result for all spaces of smaller dimension. By Theorem [7.5.1](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-1), $\varphi$ has at least one eigenvalue, say $\lambda_1$. By Proposition [7.6.9](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-9), $$V = V_{\lambda_1} \oplus U, \qquad U = \Img(\varphi - \lambda_1)^n,$$ with $U$ invariant under $\varphi$. Since $V_{\lambda_1} \neq \{0\}$, we have $\dim U < \dim V$. By the induction hypothesis applied to $\varphi|_U$, $$U = U_{\mu_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus U_{\mu_s},$$ where $\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_s$ are the eigenvalues of $\varphi|_U$ and $U_{\mu} = \ker(\varphi|_U - \mu)^{\dim U}$ are its generalized eigenspaces. An eigenvector of $\varphi|_U$ is an eigenvector of $\varphi$, so each $\mu_j$ is one of $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_\ell$; and $U_{\mu_j} \subseteq \ker(\varphi - \mu_j)^n = V_{\mu_j}$. Therefore $$V = V_{\lambda_1} + U_{\mu_1} + \cdots + U_{\mu_s} \subseteq V_{\lambda_1} + V_{\lambda_2} + \cdots + V_{\lambda_\ell},$$ so the generalized eigenspaces span $V$. The dimension formula follows because the sum is direct.
:::

:::corollary{7.6.12} The image of $(\varphi - \lambda_i)^n$
In the situation of Theorem [7.6.11](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#theorem-7-6-11), with $n = \dim V$, $$\Img(\varphi - \lambda_i)^n = \bigoplus_{j \neq i} V_{\lambda_j} \quad\text{for each } i.$$
:::

:::proof
For $j \neq i$, the operator $\varphi - \lambda_i$ maps $V_{\lambda_j}$ isomorphically onto itself (Proposition [7.6.8](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-8)(d)), so $V_{\lambda_j} = (\varphi - \lambda_i)^n(V_{\lambda_j}) \subseteq \Img(\varphi - \lambda_i)^n$. Hence $\bigoplus_{j \neq i} V_{\lambda_j} \subseteq \Img(\varphi - \lambda_i)^n$. By Proposition [7.6.9](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-9) and Theorem [7.6.11](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#theorem-7-6-11), both sides have dimension $n - \dim V_{\lambda_i}$, so they are equal.
:::

Combining the decomposition with triangular form gives a matrix in which each eigenvalue occupies its own block.

:::corollary{7.6.13} Block-triangular form
Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $\varphi \in \End(V)$, and let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_\ell$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $\varphi$, with $d_i = \dim V_{\lambda_i}$. There is a basis of $V$ in which the matrix of $\varphi$ is block diagonal, $$\mcM(\varphi) = \begin{pmatrix} A_1 & & 0 \\ & \ddots & \\ 0 & & A_\ell \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A_i = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_i & & * \\ & \ddots & \\ 0 & & \lambda_i \end{pmatrix} \in \mcM_{d_i \times d_i}(k),$$ where each $A_i$ is upper triangular with all diagonal entries equal to $\lambda_i$.
:::

:::proof
Each $V_{\lambda_i}$ is a nonzero invariant subspace. By Theorem [7.5.2](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-2), it has a basis in which $\varphi|_{V_{\lambda_i}}$ has an upper-triangular matrix $A_i$. The diagonal entries of $A_i$ are eigenvalues of $\varphi|_{V_{\lambda_i}}$ (Corollary [7.5.4](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#corollary-7-5-4)), and the only such eigenvalue is $\lambda_i$ (Proposition [7.6.8](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#proposition-7-6-8)(d)). Concatenating these bases gives a basis of $V = \bigoplus V_{\lambda_i}$, in which the matrix is block diagonal by Theorem [7.3.4](/notes/math-55a/7-3-invariant-subspaces#theorem-7-3-4).
:::

:::theorem{7.6.14} Algebraic multiplicity equals $\dim V_\lambda$
Let $k$ be algebraically closed, $\varphi \in \End(V)$, and let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_\ell$ be the distinct eigenvalues of $\varphi$. Then $$\chi_\varphi(x) = \prod_{i=1}^\ell (x - \lambda_i)^{\dim V_{\lambda_i}}.$$ Hence the algebraic multiplicity of each eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ is $\dim V_{\lambda_i}$, and the algebraic multiplicities add up to $\dim V$.
:::

:::proof
The matrix of Corollary [7.6.13](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#corollary-7-6-13) is upper triangular, and $\lambda_i$ appears on its diagonal exactly $\dim V_{\lambda_i}$ times. Apply Corollary [7.5.4](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#corollary-7-5-4)(b).
:::

:::corollary{7.6.15} Geometric and algebraic multiplicity
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and $\lambda$ an eigenvalue of $\varphi \in \End(V)$. Then $$1 \leq \dim E(\lambda, \varphi) \leq \dim V_\lambda = \text{(algebraic multiplicity of } \lambda).$$ The operator $\varphi$ is diagonalizable if and only if the geometric multiplicity equals the algebraic multiplicity for every eigenvalue, i.e., if and only if $E(\lambda, \varphi) = V_\lambda$ for every eigenvalue $\lambda$.
:::

:::proof
The inequalities follow from $\{0\} \neq E(\lambda, \varphi) \subseteq V_\lambda$ and Theorem [7.6.14](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#theorem-7-6-14). By Theorem [7.4.13](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#theorem-7-4-13), $\varphi$ is diagonalizable if and only if $\sum_i \dim E(\lambda_i, \varphi) = \dim V$, and $\dim V = \sum_i \dim V_{\lambda_i}$ by Theorem [7.6.11](/notes/math-55a/7-6-generalized-eigenspaces#theorem-7-6-11). Since $\dim E(\lambda_i, \varphi) \leq \dim V_{\lambda_i}$ for each $i$, the two sums agree if and only if every term agrees.
:::

:::example{7.6.16} Decomposition for a $3 \times 3$ matrix
Consider $\varphi : \CC^3 \to \CC^3$ with matrix $$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}.$$ The matrix is upper triangular, so $\chi_A(x) = (x-2)^2(x-3)$: the eigenvalue $2$ has algebraic multiplicity 2 and the eigenvalue $3$ has algebraic multiplicity 1.

For $\lambda = 2$: $$A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad (A-2I)^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},$$ and $(A - 2I)^3 = (A - 2I)^2$. So $V_2 = \ker(A-2I)^3 = \ker(A - 2I)^2 = \operatorname{Span}\{e_1, e_2\}$, which has dimension 2, while the eigenspace $E(2, \varphi) = \operatorname{Span}\{e_1\}$ has dimension 1.

For $\lambda = 3$: the powers of $A - 3I$ all have kernel $\operatorname{Span}\{e_3\}$, so $V_3 = E(3, \varphi) = \operatorname{Span}\{e_3\}$, of dimension 1.

Indeed, $\CC^3 = V_2 \oplus V_3$, the dimensions agree with the algebraic multiplicities, and $\varphi$ is not diagonalizable.
:::
